review:
It seems like the game is almost done so I can let out my opinions. I played both Subnautica and Subnautica: Below Zero from the beginning of their early access launches.
According to Steam I have played:
Subnautica- 100+ hrs
Subnautica: Below Zero- 60+ hrs
It's so hard for me to let go of the hope of this game being something more than what it is turning/turned out to be. To be philosophical for a moment, we are more disappointed with something that gets close to the target than we are with something that misses it completely. To me Below Zero is a large step back from the original in the ways that made the original so special. Which is a heart wrenching thing to see. I will break it down more but first I want to make sure that you, the reader of this knows that Below Zero is a good game. It's beautiful and engaging. Like the first game, it is one that is hard to stop playing. Also like the first game, Its base loop of resource gathering a tool creation is well paced and gets you to explore farther and dive deeper to find those valuable resources.
Where Below Zero falls short is in its understanding of what made the first game amazing. It is a survival game. There are A TON of survival games. But how many strictly underwater survival games are there? When the first Subnautica came out I think it was the only one. Yes it has some out of water roaming in it but it was very minimal. The atmosphere was also incredible. It takes place on an alien planet so there isn't any people roaming around. Aside from some logs there isn't any form of human life. To add to the isolation the radio guy says they are gonna rescue you and then they get blown out of the sky! If that doesn't make the atmosphere seem desperate then sprinkle in the fact that all other survivors are eaten before you get to them and you have yourself some edge of your seat suspense. Next, the first game has a huge open world. For an indie game, it's HUGE. Lastly, the survival loop was great and you really progressed to the point where you felt like a master of your domain. Yes, you need to avoid those leviathans but the game really gave the sense that you started from nothing... and now you are driving around a massive submarine!
To summarize:
1. Isolation
2. expansive underwater world
3. Eventual dominion over that world
When I look at those 3 things, they really are the base of any survival game, except for the underwater part(the unique trait of subnautica)
Now looking at Below Zero.
1. ISOLATION
Your character drops onto the planet on purpose. so right off the bat it's not about survival in the mind of the player character. Then there are audio logs everywhere. The first game had logs like I mentioned but they didn't have audio which adds alot more personality to the characters but takes away from any sense of desperation or dread. Also, there is a voice inside your head that your converses with, again removing a sense of isolation. Lastly there is a human NPC in the game, which makes you physically not alone. So the strange alien world I was in felt a bit more homely that I was anticipating when I started playing.
2. EXPANSIVE UNDERWATER WORLD
The underwater portion of this game is significantly smaller than the original, like 25%-33% the size(my estimation). Also I'd estimate that 25%-33% of Below Zero's entire world is on land. Which means they removed 25%-33% of the world that made the game unique from all other survival games. Yes, the land is still on an alien planet. But there are plenty of run around survival games on alien planets. I can't help but think of what it would of been like if that 25%-33% was put into the underwater world. Another amazing biome or 2 could have been added. Oh man...sweet, beautiful underwater biomes...
3. EVENTUAL DOMINION OVER THE WORLD
I was waiting for a giant sub like machine to be introduced into the game. The sea truck(which is a small sub) is fine, but it hardly feels like a sea conquering machine. While you do progress and climb the ladder of dominance it end really quickly. You find the sea truck withing a few hrs and then you made it. That's it. You get attachments for the sea truck(a cool idea) that lets you explore farther and longer. The attachments are things like more storage or an aquarium for storing food. But by adding attachments the truck its movement speed is reduced significantly so I usually have 1 attachment and go back to my base when I want to swap(cause the underwater world is so small it doesn't take much time). If I really need to have access to food and storage(among other attachments for the truck I wont mention) why can't I use the great base building mechanics and build small bases around the small underwater world? That would eliminate almost all of the benefits that the truck provides! 
I walk away from this game confused and sad that the developers didn't see what made the original so amazing. It's almost like they went in the opposite direction. I hope Below Zero does well because they are obviously very talented people and I want them to succeed. I also want them to try again.

Side note. Below Zero is $30!? You guys should rethink that.

It's Diet Subnautica, not Subnautica 2.

Had I not played the original Subnautica first, I would have thought this was a pretty great game, and likely wouldn't have had any issues with it at all. But I did play the original first, and that set the bar for my expectations -- especially given that the two games are the same price.

It's gorgeous. The coding is tighter, the animations are smoother, it is WAY better optimized -- no more chugging and chunking while distant objects struggle to render. The weather effects are great, and the addition of temperature as a survival mechanic is neat. There is a lot of new lore (with an interesting cast of characters), plenty of new flora and fauna to scan, great new base building pieces, and a lot of new decor options.

Now here comes the bad:

The map is TINY compared to the original. And extremely shallow -- you can go almost everywhere that matters with the first depth module for the seatruck and a bit of free diving.

The survival elements feel poorly balanced. I got the tank upgrades very quickly, and never felt concerned with hunger or thirst thanks to slightly overtuned edible plants being so easy to access, and food/water being in so many of the numerous crates scattered across the map.

The progression curve feels flat compared to the first game -- the upgrades come too quickly, and don't feel as rewarding. The Cyclops allowed you to go DEEP. Well, there is no "deep" to explore, here. And no reason to do so anyway, as all the endgame crafting materials are very plentiful and are able to be picked up very early in.

You unlock some things at weird times. Some too early (like the multipurpose room), some too late (like the decorative plant walls -- which you can only scan from one specific area, despite encountering them in more than one place).

You are able to scan a lot of new plants, but the ones you can actually take seeds/samples from and grow for yourself are EXTREMELY limited. Why? Even if they were just decorative elements at your base, with no other use, that would still be SOMETHING. There aren't many creature eggs to find, either. It almost feels like the game was pushed out early, with less content than originally planned.

Props from the first game are used as decor in the second game, but are unable to be scanned or picked up (all the lab equipment, many island plants). This makes no sense to me. The assets are already there, in use in the game world. Slap an inventory icon on it and let us use them!

There aren't many uses for the spy pengling. At all. It could have added a lot of exploration value, but it's mostly a waste of inventory space. Same for the snowfox, which I used approximately once and then discarded -- it really needed to be able to hover on water, to make it worth zipping around on.

There aren't as many leviathans, and they aren't as scary. The game in general isn't as scary. I never felt alone. I never got lost in an utterly black void, a cave system some 1000m down, unable to orient myself and running out of air, water, or flashlight battery.

The player character legit sounds like she is edging a big fat orgasm when she eats (UNNHHHH, MMMMM, AAAHHH). There is no way someone didn't bring this up during playtesting. It is absolutely ridiculous.

Overall, it's fun and polished enough (and I got it cheaply enough) for me to give it a thumbs up. But if you pay full price for this and expect it to be just like the first one, you're gonna be disappointed -- there just isn't enough of it. Once they finish backporting the building elements from this game into the original and fixing up the older code, I'll never touch this game again.

tl;dr - Super pretty, but it feels like a DLC, not a sequel.

Compared to the first Subnautica, I feel like there are numerous minor improvements in this one. The most notable being the fact that it feels far less grindy when gathering materials. Materials are spaced in a much better fashion and are not nearly as annoying to collect. There are also numerous sections that are designed for you to have to navigate without a vehicle early on using plants that give about 30 sec of oxygen and take time to recharge that add a lot to the feel of the game. The AI for many of the creatures also appears to be significantly better than in the first game, although they still run into walls. There's a much heavier focus on story in this one as well, and the writing is quite good at times. I overall think this game has much more interesting designs on many of the creatures (although others fall flat), but it has nothing on the scale of the Sea Dragon or Emperor from the first game, which I found disappointing.

There are also quite a few things this one doesn't do as well as the first game unfortunately. I don't know if there are actually less creatures in the world, but it feels as though there are. Some environments feel just as interesting as in the first game, but others feel very bland once you spend some time in them. The crystal caves at the end have fantastic visual and level design, but aside from the (very cool) shadow leviathans, there's nothing new or special about the area really. It mostly contains the same creatures you'll find in numerous other locations. The following red crystal area is even smaller and more disappointing in that regard. It's just one big loop effectively, with the same creatures as the preceding area for the most part. Squid Sharks are particularly cool in my opinion, but they get heavily overused. The shadow leviathans are awesome, but they effectively just fill the same role as ghost leviathans in the first game. The other major ocean threat leviathan in the game has an interesting design, but doesn't even begin to inspire the fear that the reaper leviathan does in the first game. There are also few less of them than reapers, which leads to most of the ocean feeling relatively safe, which is a shame.

The place where this game suffers the most is the place where it deviates the most from its predecessor - the land gameplay. It's simply not very good. The animations on land are still very stiff and there's no option to crouch. The snow fox is cool, but flips easily and you'll spend half the time getting knocked off of it by the ice worms. The ice worms themselves are too on the nose and lack any real suspense. I was never afraid they were coming - it was obvious they were and they were more of a nuisance than an actual threat. I thought the land environment was very interesting and well designed, but the gameplay just doesn't support it well. There are numerous mechanics that work great under water that just don't translate (or look good) on land.

Overall it's a great game and I would recommend it. But, I would recommend the first one more. During the first part of this game, I was very immersed and was even enjoying myself more than the first game, but after only a short time it felt very small. Without an equivalent for reapers to box you in, there's really not much you can't just go explore very quickly, and it's far less scary of a game once you get familiar with it. There are also no major events like the Aurora exploding or the Skybeam (or whatever it's called) getting shot down, making the game feel less active as it progresses. The later areas are far less mysterious and interesting than the final zones in the first game. The alien sites are much less impressive and much less interesting, which is a shame considering the focus on alien sites in this one.  If you like the first game, you'll probably like this one, but if you haven't played the first game and are deciding on one or the other, get the first game.

If you loved the original Subnautica, you'll at least like this game. I found that, throughout my entire play through, the whole experience didn't feel nearly as mysterious and terrifying as the first game. In BZ, they replaced the huge, open map with a small, almost linear one. While some may like that, I didn't personally; I loved the huge areas of purely dark water with no visible bottom (obviously excluding the void) and the excitement of exploring these uncharted waters. In BZ, however, since there was an entire team of scientists, engineers, etc. in the area to begin with, it feels like the entire map's already been explored, which discouraged me from exploring it. The biomes don't feel nearly as unique as they did in Subnautica; they almost blend together. 

The story is okay. It's nothing life changing. Now, the original's wasn't either, but it was at least different. There are two main story lines in BZ: the one regarding the death of Robin's sister and the one about helping AL-AN. The latter has an interesting ending, and goes into the Architects in greater detail, but the one with Sam is just boring. I didn't care at all about the Sam story line; I had no incentive to find out what happened to her. It was, frankly, boring.

Overall, if you loved the original  you should definitely try BZ; while it's not as good, it gives you more of the Subnautica experience, but in a different fashion. While the original is a 10/10, BZ is probably a 7/10 for me.

In short - it's a great game, well worth your time, with a slightly different feel to the original.

Please don't make the mistake of comparing it to the first game. It's fair to say that most everyone interested in this one will have tried the first one. If you're not played either, it's definitely better to start with the first Subnautica. The reason is, and this is why there are alot of thumbs up reviews here that are "disappointed" in this follow up - there is no way you will ever recapture the feeling of awe and wonderment at being dumped into the middle of a hostile mysterious world and left to fend for yourself. You've had it in the first game (and if not, go experience it) and you will not get it back - there is nothing the devs could have done short of wiping your memory, so they decided to try something a little different. And the game is better for it.

The core of the gameplay is the same as the predecessor - you're violently thrust into a world you know nothing about, with nothing to your name but a waypoint to a pod which will be your first home. From there you explore, collect, craft and thrive. Your exploration is limited only to oxygen capacity for yourself, crush depth for your vehicle and fear of the unknown (or known).

So what's changed? One change is apparent from the get go - your character isn't a mute, she has a voice and opinions. She has her own goals to accomplish - which you can ignore if you want. There are also now humanoid NPC's you can interact with. Audio logs usually have character portraits. All contribute to make you the player feel somewhat less isolated that before.
Another change is more emphasis on land exploration, complete with monsters and terrible weather that will make short work of you if you're unprepared. There's a lengthy section, mandatory for story completion, that will make you dream of diving back into the water - remeniscent of being stuck in a blizzard surrounded by bears. Which is by no means a bad thing, I enjoyed that part exactly because I didn't know where I was - I was making progress - and I was under-equipped and close to being overwhelmed by the hostile terrain. Upon reaching my goal I realised I now had to go back the way I came which was annoying to contemplate and exhilirating to execute, as I had no means of defence against the monsters and had to outwit them.

Which brings me to another fine point - you are very free to attack this hostile terrain however you want. Careful observation and diligent exploration can make you pretty much untouchable. The monsters I mentioned? There are two ways you can discover to deal with them that will make them a non issue. But you don't have to - buy the time I found those two ways, I never had to deal with them again. And it was tricky, and it was fun. There are so many tools at your disposal, it's sometimes easy to forget that some can be used to solve problems in very creative ways.

Some reviewers mentioned the size of the game as a negative, compared to the first. I disagree. It's not as big, but it doesn't matter. It's the right size for the story it's telling. The different biomes felt unique and fantastical with a shade of real world basis for all of them. Having completed the game it didn't feel like there should have been more for the sake of it - it's a complete package, and it works. The first game achieved a sense of vast isolation with the massive, mostly empty landscapes in about a third of it's biomes, which contributed to the creepiness factor. That's gone - and it wouldn't have worked here. You'd have to go back to a mute protagonist and tone down the story, and everyone would say it was too much like the predecessor but not as good anyway. By the way, the biomes, with the audio cues, are sometimes jaw dropping.

So what sucks? Well most of my problems were tied to navigation. The first part of the game is spot on, no problems there. You explore, you get waypoints, you figure stuff out, great. But later on you don't get no waypoint. Fair enough, you have to listen, remember, figure stuff out. You can find at least 2 maps ingame that help. So let's take a particular section, one of the outdoor icy ones, a section they drew you a map for. Just like the other blizzard bit described above, I was well unprepared, making it by the skin of my teeth. Except this bit wasn't facing in one direction. It was twisty, full of caves, full of bears I had no way to deal with (that i knew), hailstones dropping every 30 secs and snow fog. Was there something at the end? Dunno, I was circling around for ages in the foggy blizzard and had no idea where I was or where the end was. It was one of two times I looked up a wiki - it was confusing and frustrating - so very unlike the worm one, that one was fun because i was making progress.

Another example - in the main plot you're asked to find 3 mcguffins. Two get a waypoint. One doesn't. I was in that area, with two leviathans biting at my bumbags, for absolute aeons, and were it not for the wiki I believe I'd still be there, circling, gently weeping. So that's 2. Not too shabby, because the rest of the game I was just stumbling around exploring and managed to hit pretty much all the story beats organically. And it was a fantastic experience.

Oh and for those saying the main characters' motivations are swept by the wayside as the main plot opens up, which makes it redundant, i'd disagree. It's not forced on you, which is a good thing, and as some have mentioned they didn't much care for it anyway. But it is important enough to be acknowledged at the end, so treat it as an optional main plot thread, rather than a main quest turned into side quest.

So there it is, don't listen to the critics, I thought I was going to hate the talky protagonist and the reduced world size, and I have to admit I was wrong - it works! Don't think of it as a sequel - it's not. Think of it more like a different flavoured "Tales of Subnautica" parallel game, go in with an open mind, and enjoy, I did

The original Subnautica is one of my favourite games of all time (with 25+ years of gaming under my belt) and so Below Zero had some incredibly high expectations to meet.

Given that it is NOT an expansion to the original but rather a completely new game I expected bigger and better things but unfortunately it doesn't deliver on this. I've not checked the actual size but the map feels much smaller and the biomes less diverse. While the Prawn suit still exists (albeit with a reduced number of modules), the Seamoth and Cyclops are gone - replaced with the Seatruck which IMO is a bit 'meh'. The Cyclops was a great end-game vehicle and something to aim for, but now we're stuck with the Seatruck which you get relatively early on and just upgrade throughout the game.

There's also (what feels like) much more gameplay above ground which, IMO, kind of defeats the whole Subnautica theme of being set underwater. 

I bought this very early in it's Early Access release and I'm on my 3rd playthrough now that more content is added. Don't get me wrong, it's still a great game that I would absolutely recommend but it is unfortunately overshadowed by the original which will take some beating.

This review is spoiler-free.

I'm a big fan of the original Subnautica, but I'd heard a lot of people say Below Zero 'isn't as good' so I was hesitant. I'm discerning about what games I choose to buy and spend my time playing. I obviously ended up getting it though and I just finished a very 'no rush' playthrough. If you're in a similar position to where I was, this is the review for you.

First, where I'm coming from. My favorite part of Subnautica was the unique balance of open-world exploration, self-paced storytelling, and plain, primal terror (not to be confused with horror). I also found the plot interesting and it held my attention, and I only found it more intriguing and believable for the slowness with which you discover details and the lack of direction each discovery left you with as to where you go next, and the incompleteness of what you learn. And, I loved the graphics and environment - the graphics are not very technically impressive, but the developers made beautiful, compelling things with what they had, and that is worth infinitely more than any amount of polygons on a screen or pixels in a texture.

From the start, Below Zero is not set up the same way at all, and that's totally fine. It doesn't come even close to feeling linear, and it doesn't hold your hand per se, but it starts you off knowing why you are here and with some idea of where to go. You are given most of what you need to start digging into the plot's mysteries fairly early on in the game, in terms of both technology and story information, and it falls to you to use those things to explore and connect the dots. It does present its story in a similar way though: most of what you get comes as logs and wrecks, and you piece it together yourself.

My only plot-related complaint would be that the story played up the dystopian transgovernmental corporation that is Alterra a little bit too much, to the point of being a bit caricaturesque at a couple points, only to have Alterra just disappear which I think is extremely out of character for an organization in their position (I can't say more without spoiling anything). It's not really that big a deal and I'm probably giving it more text than it's worth, but you notice it after you stop playing and you you contemplate the events of the game, and it does break up the story just a little bit.

Now, the progression is one area where the original Subnautica was perhaps flawless: the equipment you 'unlock', the new environments you push into, and the new threats you face are all balanced spectacularly. Below Zero definitely comes up short. A huge part of the reason - you knew this was coming - is the Seatruck. I don't think a comparison to the Cyclops is valid so I won't try to force one, but the Seamoth is fair game. And I think the early game Seatruck compares fine to the Seamoth in practice; slap a storage module on the back just like you stuck hardcases to the side of your Seamoth, and you're good to go explore areas you would have struggled to reach before (or did struggle but did it anyway, now you can go back). As you go, you discover upgrades and new modules that add functionality to the Seatruck... in theory. The implementation just isn't great. Give it enough modules and upgrades that hauling a Prawn suit along and trying to use it as a roving base makes any real sense, and it turns into an awkward balance of zippy but clunky, the poor storage capacity is simply frustrating, and the Prawn never feels really necessary. You can use it that way, and you probably will, but it never turns into anything that makes it feel more useful or powerful or rewarding than it did early in the game. It just ends up getting old and being mildly annoying. It probably seems like I'm harping on this vehicle, but Below Zero is built with the Seatruck as a core part of its gameplay, and for something that essential, it isn't as well done as I'd hope.

Then there are the bugs. The original Subnautica had a few - I'm sure you've been trapped in a Prawn suit, or beached your Seamoth as a means of parking and come back to find it 10m under the ground. But Below Zero is riddled with minor graphical bugs that let you see through ledges and see certain things from absurd distances and cause weird and very noticeable lighting issues. It also has quite a few spots you can accidentally trap yourself on terrain geometry and essentially softlock the game, and that even happens in areas that are important to the plot in places you are likely to go through (often you can save yourself by looking down and placing a light stick, if you keep one on you like I do). And there's one particular mean leviathan in one particular area that has a nasty habit of getting out of bounds and then coming at you through the ground or ceiling once or twice before getting back in bounds and on its normal path, which is stupefyingly scary but also extremely immersion-breaking and frustrating. The result of all this is a game that feels unpolished... not unfinished, just unpolished.

And on a similar note, Below Zero doesn't feel quite as fleshed-out as the original either. There were something like three dozen species of plants you could harvest in Subnautica, just plants, and most of them had absolutely no practical use whatsoever. And there were bunches of little pieces of useless equipment and glass containers and bags and all kinds of other things lying around you could pick up and keep like some kind of sea/space raccoon. All this let you decorate your base and make it feel more like home using the things you found in the world. Below Zero has tons of neat-looking plants and all kinds of equipment to give depth to the biomes and locations you find, but it only lets you have what is useful so you can't bring that depth home. All it adds in return is a bunch of posters and picture frames, and a bunch of options for bedspreads and a faux wooden desk in the habitat builder. This isn't a problem per se, but let's face it, we all enjoyed the crap out of sprucing up our seabases and turning them into a sort of home beyond just a place to store materials and fabricate components, and Below Zero takes an important part of that away which leaves it feeling disproportionately spartan.
Plus, probably more importantly, there's no wondering what you might want to collect in your travels; if you can pick it up or harvest it, you should keep it around, especially if it isn't edible. Below Zero also has quite a few large plants and/or plant-like things you can't even scan, where that was unusual in the original, so that's a bit weird too, and it becomes more frequent and more noticeable in the 2-3 late game areas which is... *narrows eyes*... interesting.

I realize I just wrote a short essay criticizing Below Zero's issues and shortcomings, but that's because I think it's good enough to be worth criticizing. Most of my gripes are fairly minor, and most are probably fixable via updates.

Below Zero also does some very important things right. It gives us a whole new world of unique and beautiful environments to explore and ecosystems to see, complete with the occasional moment of terror as the world reminds you that you are small and fragile and there are places you do not belong. It gives a story with interesting, flawed, and dynamic main characters, and a compelling overall arc that the original doesn't compete with. I enjoyed this game and I am glad I played it.

Bottom line here. If you enjoyed Subnautica and you want more, Below Zero will probably scratch that itch quite nicely. Frankly, I don't think it's quite as good as the original, but it's not too far off.
If you haven't played the original because you are daunted by the 'wander aimlessly' premise, Below Zero doesn't do that for the most part so you should be fine, and it will kind of teach you how to survive the original game too. Otherwise, I'd probably recommend you play the original first and get this only if you do like it.

I'm giving this a thumbs down, but I'd really rather give it a "meh" (thumb to the side) - it's just not an option.

The original game was huge, they got everything right. Unfortunately, with "Below Zero", some of the things that were the "most right" in the original were dropped. 
It's like removing the meat from a burger and replacing it with - I don't know - more bread?

The worst change for me is the transition from the mute character, that forced me to think by myself and, as a direct result, made me actually BE that character, into a talking puppet, that can't seem to shut up and thinks my thoughts for me. This detaches the player from the character and totally ruins the immersive effect of BEING that character. I'm degraded to controlling somebody else.

The second worst flaw (though it might as well share the first place with the talking puppet) is that modular truck thing.
I totally get, that it must have sounded very promising on paper. But then it feels like they went on to develop one module after another.
And by the time anyone would have figured out, that it's just not really working (with it's unnatural, unrealistic handling based on the seamoth and the uselessness of many of its modules and its clunkyness and its total lack of impressiveness....), I assume it would have required balls to admit that and scrap it, simply write off the time it took to get there.

Many (most) will agree, that the Cyclops was THE big achievement in Subnautica. It was a mighty thing, I loved the voice of its AI, its handling, that gave you the feeling of captaining a huge vessel to go deep down...
So with this being the pinnacle of vehicle achievements in Subnautica, let's scrap that in "Below Zero", shall we? After all, we have a crappy sea truck.

Speaking of deep down. Wasn't that great, that the further the game progressed, you had to go deeper and deeper into more and more dangerous areas? Sound effects, that would give you goose bumps (my son frequently asked me to take over the controls when he found it too chilling to do by himself)?
Below Zero comes off as a nice snorkeling trip. No suspense, the atmosphere is simply dull.

If Below Zere were part one, I'd say it's a great promising game - and the original Subnautica being the sequel, I'd say "now you nailed it!".
But the way it is, I'd recommend: play the original twice and skip this one.

The original subnautica is one of my favorite games of all time. I say this because I want to be clear from the start that Everything I say here comes from a genuine place of love for this series.

Below Zero is a fantastic game. I had this game for 2 1/2 years before I actually decided to hunker down and do it. My problem in all my previous attempts was that I expected just Subnautica: The Rerun. This game may be great, but it is very different. It took a while for me to accept those differences and recognize the beauty of this game.

I'll start with some objective positives. The visuals in this game are downright stunning. The creatures and areas you come across, especially in the deeper biomes, are some of the most visually interesting and pleasing I have ever seen. I will try to limit spoilers, but there is one creature in particular who is incredibly unique and you can even go into it to harvest resources. It is some of the most interesting sci-fi I have ever seen. If you enjoyed the unique creatures in the original, they only get better, and the graphics follow suit.

Another total victory on Below Zero's part is the music. The music and ambiance in this game is great. The music present in each biome sets a perfect musical tone for what to expect. The devs have also added in a few songs from fans of the original game that you can play. A nice little treat for the fans.

Now, one major difference between this game and the previous is what I will simply refer to as space. The original subnautica excelled at really exploiting the fear of what we cannot see. The game is really open and spacious There are plenty of points when you will look down and see nothing but blue or black. You have little to no idea of what will be waiting in the depths until you choose to go down, or you just constantly stick to the floor to always know where you are. It's very reminiscent of the real ocean.

This game is much "shallower" although I don't think that is technically the right word. There are very few times where you will look into the abyss and see nothing. There will almost always be a floor or rock or creatures not too far away. It is a very different experience. Now, it is less a fear of what you cannot see, but more of a fear of what you can. You are always seeing something that is a threat. The game also has a greater focus on enclosed cave systems and tight spaces, preying on one's claustrophobia, which is not helped by some massive carnivore circling above. It turns the game almost into a strategic board game, having to keep your precious truck out of harms way. It turns into a very different experience compared to the original. If you go in expecting wide open spaces like before, you may end up like I did and think the game is not good.

Overall, Below Zero is a fantastic game in its own right. There are plenty more good aspects I could mention. The seatruck (or as i call it, the Fjord F-150) for example is implemented great. It is not perfect, some things are hard to figure out naturally and some places are a bit hard to build in, but overall is a great experience. If you liked the previous game, love the ocean, love open world survival games, or all of the above, you will love this game. But, if you love the original a bit too much like me, give this game a chance to make the experience its own.

These games are both master classes in open world survival. They are different, but they go together.

TL;DR I really wanted to like Below Zero, but its clear the studio has no idea what made the original "tick". 

[h1]Story[/h1]
It was unfortunately entirely derivative, obnoxious, and only ever served to break immersion and disrupting player agency by making "im15andthisisdeep" level statements from the player character. The forced statements overrides any chance of developing a ludo-narrative (an emergent story driven by gameplay). It surely must have cost a lot of resources to make given the scope of the studio, which were unfortunately wasted entirely. Bad Netflix-like stereotypical dialogue and characters, an incredulous overabundance of "badass" female characters [spoiler](the crashed ships captain is literally called "Captain Badass", sans any self-awareness)[/spoiler] The Degasi crew from the original represented one of the highlights, a simple but engaging story that paralleled player experience, gradually discovering their fate as the player explored and the planet. [spoiler]Discovering that each of them ultimately suffered a tragic but fitting death, helped underline the grim reality of planet 4546B. Come Below Zero however, not content with ruining its own worldbuilding, takes the "badass" female character Marguerita from the Degasi crew, and retcons her into having survived miraculously thereby ruining the poetic ending of the original. Maybe if she played a crucial part in the story, which seems to be the case initially - but as it turns out this story-thread is sidetracked entirely in favour of an Architect alien storyline.[/spoiler]

Which brings us to what is revealed to be the main storyline, the discovery and consequent interaction with [spoiler]the alien AL-AN character.[/spoiler] Intriguing at first, it soon becomes apparent that it trivializes the ENTIRE point of the game. All possible exploration is now moot, because every [spoiler]Architect location[/spoiler] is given it's own fat juicy marker. Besides one or two final locations for the story which are impossible to miss due to it being located underneath [spoiler]Marguerita's base[/spoiler], everything gets pointed out. What is left, is an world without any sense mystery or scope. [spoiler]In exchange we get a run-of-the-mill goofy robot "what is love" interaction dialogue, that ultimately leads to the conclusion of the game, as the alien offers to bring us along to its homeworld. Our character can simply hop on board, as I did, only to realize after traveling through a well made closing sequence - I never actually "solved" the original storyline to completion. Oh well, my strong independent gay engineer genius sister died pointlessly, after having fabricated a cure in 5 minutes for a disease that an alien super AI couldn't cure in a thousand years. Yet despite having this cure she opted to blow up the remaining source with explosives (because evil company bad) and ends up killing herself and an innocent coworker, because... reasons???. [/spoiler] 

Lastly, in the original Subnautica, the excellent writing of the PDA-AI assistant added a crucial amount of  flavour and humour to the world. For some (obviously contemporary political) reason this has now been given an indian accent, which is whatever, but the unique sense of humour is lacking entirely.

[h1]Dangers[/h1]
These are now entirely toothless, there is no actual depth to the world, and consequently to the game, creatures are copy-pasted across the biomes. While they are well designed on a technical level, they are overrused - depriving them of their unique character. Consequently, very few locations felt unique, the only "deep" location of the game was entirely enclosed and therefore lacking the feeling of the unknown. The new Leviathan in the deep area is nicely designed, but due to the limited space of the location, you are basically forced into being attacked by it, and soon you realize it barely does damage. 

[h1]Base building[/h1]
The only positive compared to the original, adding and expanding on the existing great base building options. Unfortunately these felt meaningless due to the lack of depth or variety in the world. I only expanded towards the one location near the deep cave, but soon realized it just contained [spoiler]two easily reached story events without anything else.[/spoiler] There was never any actual need to build a base there. I could've reached it without any vehicles as it turned out. 

[h1]Sound[/h1]
Sound design was mostly decent, not quite as inspired musically or tonally as the original but worthy enough for a sequel. However, one major issue kept jumping out - they "crocodile / lizard" like creatures had an obvious bugged biting noise which reached way beyond to what it should. It absolutely destroyed immersion, and was it was surprising to see this obvious bug unfixed after such a long time after full release. 

[h1]Land exploration[/h1]
The new cold system started out decently, having potential to add a new element of danger to land travel, inverting the original experience of land offering some recluse from the hostile world below. However, this new survival element becomes harmless almost immediately through the overabundance of frost peppers, which give you all that you'd ever need without having even the most basic of protective gear or vehicles. The new land vehicle looks cool but is somehow less controllable than a Warthog in Halo 1, and despite "floating" it manages to hit everything on its path. Its only use is to serve as a magic heater, and is entirely trivialized by the prawn suit, offering no benefits compared to the latter. The great looking Land Leviathan creature soon becomes predictable as it's clearly reduced to static "trigger" areas without any feeling of being sentient or it being capable of giving chase. Not to mention the low quality interaction it has with the new land vehicle. 

[h1]Subnautica[/h1] 
The power of the original was its combination of survival, exploration and overcoming the immense looming fear that the unknown depths summoned, with little story notes and soundbites sprinkled across. The PC was a typical silent protagonist, surely due to budgetary restraints, which had the added benefit of aiding player agency and immersion. Instead of being shoehorned into listening to some badly written Netflix derivative garbage, I could simply [b]be[/b] the player without any explicit character identifiers overriding immersion. 

Danger seemed to be everywhere, and as I became familiar with the layout of the world and its creatures, I gradually overcame this fear. Each biome would offer something new entirely, with clear character, new creatures with new challenges and opportunities. Behaviour to study and be fascinated by. Exploration felt meaningful because something could be hidden [b]anywhere[/b]. With progress gated behind depth it allowed for a nice gradual progression, as my technology improved, I was able to uncover more of the world and its simple but engaging story. 

In the end, I was fully familiar with the world and able to travel around it comfortably, now fully feeling in control. I looked back on the planet with a sense of pride and joy. 

Yes, there were certainly things that could've been improved on in the original. But instead of improving upon the original, Below Zero seems to purposfully try to dampen the stengths of the original. As so often happens to studios as they grow, they all want to be Naughty Dog and basically make a linear Hollywood narrative, forgetting that what made their studio rise in the first place was not the linear narrative, but the player-driven ludo-narrative. But instead of enhancing the ludo-narrative, they've chosen to pursue pointless contemporaneous goals. 

[i]"My disappointment is immeasurable and my day is ruined."[/i]

I played and beat subnautica 1 for the first time a few weeks before the release of below zero. After playing and finishing both back to back, It's very very clear to me something happened to Below Zero in development that took a winning formula from the first game and twisted it into an unrecognizable mess. In no particular order, I will go over my issues:

1.) Story - The first game combined story telling with gameplay seamlessly. You have instant motivation and direction from the first second of taking control of the playable character. and that wasn't because you had some magical being in your head telling you where to go and why youre going there. It feels like Below Zero has 2 different stoies crammed into 1 and as a result, neither side gets the attention it needs and ends up feeling like both stories are unfinished and uninteresting. You have the story of AL-AN the alien and the story of Robin (you) and Sam (your sister). Al-AN's story is mildly interesting because it adds to the lore from the first game but, thats the only reason it has any interest (a common theme I've noticed). Sam's and Robin's Story is the whole reason youre on the planet in the first place and everything is pretty much told to you within the first hour of starting the game. This story just dropped off the face of the planet as soon as you meet AL-AN.

2.) Map/materials - The map design for BZ compared to the first is just garbage. The first game anchored your internal compass to the auroara then it generally kept changing biomes the further down you would go. On top of that, the transitions between biomes generally made sense. In BZ the biomes are seemingly randomly squished together with very little landmarks or uniqueness to orient yourself. Every spot in the crystal caves looks like every other spot in the crystal caves, every spot in the purple fissures looks like every other spot in the purple fissures, ect ect. The materials you use have this problem too. You find just about everything you need outside of magnitite and the blue crystals in the area you find AL-AN in, which is probably where everyone builds their first base.

3.) Land/temp meter - So the 2 biggest aspects to BZ that I gathered was a larger focus on land exploration and an additional survival mechanic in the form of a temp meter. After beating the game, I do not understand why they did this. The temp meter really only has any change when you are on land and wasnt a factor even a little bit under the water which makes 0 sense to me. When you are on land, dont worry as there are about 3 heat flowers every 10 steps you take so youll never run into an issue with freezing. After getting the prawn suit (which you can get within the first hour easily) it becomes an even bigger non issue. As for the land aspect, what a bore. Theres less to see on the 3 islands in this game than there was on the 2 islands in the first game. Everything above water is frozen so its all white and when its not thats because its storming or hailing or something and you just cant see anything. There are a ton of "land" survival exploration games to play that do it way better because they are geared for it. Subnautica is at its best in the water and thats clearer than its ever been after spending as much time on land as you do in BZ.

4.) Survival - It wasnt particularly difficult to survive in the first game but BZ its almost impossible not to survive. Somehow its easier to procure food in a freezing climate than the more temperate climate of the first game. Who knew? You get the potatoes and watermelons from the first game but add on to that peppers, nuts, fruits growing under ice and more nutrient bars than youll ever need. Theres even an over abundance of air assistance even though you can get the max air tank pretty early on. You have o2 trees everywhere, fish that give o2 everywhere, and rock outcroppings that act similar to the o2 plants from the first game. On top of all of this, you unlock a chest that acts like the ender chest in minecraft where its shared with other ender chests so you can rest assured even in a pinch youll always be able to survive and if you run out in your chest just use the instant teleporter device that instantly teleports you back to your seatruck. Way too easy.

5.) Vehicles - There is no vehicle progression in BZ. You use the sea truck for all of 20 minutes before unlocking the prawn suit and once you have the prawn suit thats it. You dont need anything else. The upgrades are cheap and theres plunty of storage you can add on to ensure youre never low on supplies. On top of that the prawn suit makes all of the land sections a joke and you casually jump past the "scary" worm without breaking a sweat. You unlock modules for the sea truck that turn it into more of the cyclops from the first game but its not like you could take it anywhere. Its so slow and cumbersome and it will not fit into the places you need to go. The prawn suit fits everywhere you need to go and youll only make a trip deeper than 400m or so maybe 2 times so its not like you need the mobile base aspects of the cyclops like sea truck.

6.) Glitches - I played the first game years after it came out so im sure it was patched to fix glitches and such but this game has a ton. At least 1 serious one that I found and 2-3 map glitches (on land of course) where I fell out of the map. The serious glitch was towards the very end after you assemble AL-ANs body, my prawn suit just vanished. I reloaded my save and repeated this process with the same effect 5 times before I found a spot to put the prawn suit far enough away that it was still there after the cutscene. I was under the impression early access was designed to eliminate these kinds of glitches. 

7.) Base building - This was the only area of the game that I think actually improved from the first game (although not much). They added a larger room and more stuff to put in it although that stuff is primarily cosmetic. They even added a new room with the control room but it doesnt actually do anything. It just gives you some minor information like the time of day and your power use. It would have been nice to actually get some room additions that had some greater purpose. For instance (minor spoiler) [spoiler] I think it would have been cooler to have to build a fabrication room for the purpose of getting AL-ANs body than just bringing the materials to the room in the crystal caves to build it. [/spoiler] 

8.) Leviathin designs - These guys are laughable in BZ. They dont deal much damage, they dont chase that hard, and they arent threatening. There is no dragon or sea empress in BZ. You can casually just swim on by the sea life in this game much like the worm i mentioned on land. Even if one of them catches you in your prawn suit, theyd have to do it 4 more times for it to matter.

All in all i dont really know where all the development went for this. I saw a video from someone playing it at like the end of 2019 and it looked like a much more complete game somehow than the one launched like a year and a half later. I think with the way this ended up, BZ would have been much better as an add on to the first game for like 10-15 bucks in the same map with the same character as the first game with the AL-AN story added in and the extra base building aspects added in.

Having played through the first game multiple times, I decided to return to Below Zero again. I had remembered fans of the first game having disliked Below Zero and didn't really understand all the hate the first time I played the game through. After finishing (not completing, but decidedly not returning to) my second play through, I can safely say that I get it now.

Here's everything wrong with the game:

1. Progression - Progression in Below Zero is completely uneven. Maybe twenty minutes into my run, I had found Outpost Zero and scanned several blueprints that would be considered mid-late game in the original Subnautica. I don't think I even had a Seaglide yet, let alone a builder tool. This phenomenon continued throughout the game, and I often felt simultaneously over and under geared.

The depth mechanic that facilitated progression in the first game is pretty much non-existent in Below Zero; you can comfortably navigate about 80% of the (meaningful) map with a basic Seatruck, Seaglide, and Oxygen plants. As a result, there's no real order in which you gather blueprints and experience events, and it makes the whole experience very disjointed.

2. Characters - one of the biggest changes from the original is greater focus on characters and dialogue. This wouldn't be an issue if the characters weren't all unlikable, childish, one-dimensional caricatures. The writing is absolutely awful, and I felt embarrassed for the voice actors every time I listened to a recording. I completely understand Alterra's decision to stick all of these people together out in the middle of icy nowhere.

Robin is a whiny, jaded know-it-all, and her conversations with Alan sound like something out of an undergrad philosophy dormitory common room. I don't even know the name of the protagonist from the original game, but after a few of these conversations I thank him wholeheartedly for keeping his mouth shut throughout the first adventure. Love that guy!

3. Large Areas - While many of the new biomes are great (Twisty Bridges, Lily Pads), there are some infuriatingly large, empty areas that the game forces you to slog through. The two overland areas essentially serve to be as annoying as possible to get all the way through, just to grab the one thing you need and never return. They are large seemingly for the sole purpose of being time-consuming and confusing to navigate; that's the challenge. There is an alien gateway shortcut in one of these overland sections that literally takes longer to utilize than just walking to the end destination - what?!

Don't worry though - large, useless areas aren't just limited to the land. The end-game deep biomes are just as huge and empty as the overland areas. Subnautica's Lost River was undeniably huge, but despite it's name I never remember actually getting lost. The tunnel does a good job of guiding you to the end of the game. The deep areas in Below Zero are twisting networks of interconnected caverns that all look the same, and I found myself going around in circles until I managed to get lucky and find the tiny little area the game had me looking for.

4. Boring, Annoying Leviathans - the Reaper put Subnautica on the map, I don't care what anyone says. There are areas in the first game I still haven't been to after maybe a dozen playthroughs because those things are so terrifying (although pretty manageable in the end). Leviathans in Below Zero are the opposite. Save for the Vent Garden (that thing is awesome, maybe the best five minutes of the game), the new Leviathans are all unintimidating and incredibly frustrating to manage.

Remember what I said about the huge, empty deep zones? I forgot to mention that, while cruising around in circles looking for the next place to go, you're going to get grabbed by the Shadow Leviathan roughly every thirty seconds, spend the next thirty seconds repairing your ship, travel maybe 100 meters, then rinse and repeat. ALL THE WAY DOWN! Unlike the Ghost Leviathans, the Shadow Leviathans can pull you out of any tiny crevice; there is no escape.

In the end, this is what killed my playthrough. I got to the last area deep down at the bottom of the map, only for the game to inform me that I needed to turn around and brave the onslaught of Shadow Leviathans again to collect the wide variety of resources I'd need to complete the game. It was at that point, having re-experienced Below Zero to my (dis)satisfaction, that I decided to power down and call it quits. I can only pray that Robin stays in that deep dark cave at the bottom of the sea and never has a chance to run a power drill between another player's ears ever again.

Subnautica is not a game for everyone, to be sure. There are no guns. It does not hold your hand and tell you explicitly where to go or what you should be doing. You often wonder, "Am I doing the right thing?" while you swim around exploring the beautiful world, barely caring one way the other. What Unknown Worlds have done is create a living, breathing world that you are sad to leave when it's over. When it concluded, I felt richer for the experience, but a little dimmer. I wished to go back in time and experience the game for the first time again. 

Then came Below Zero, and my wish was granted! This is not just another biome or a small DLC. This is a sequel, or at least it will be. Obviously it's in VERY early access and much of the game is still in development. Don't think of this as a bad thing; think of it as keeping you from devouring this incredible experience all in one sitting. Help the devs make the game. Be a part of the community. In certain spots in the game, you'll see a message from the devs asking for community suggestions and input. Very rarely will a video game give you fun and make you feel happiness like this.  

As for the quality of the game, it's already promising. The color palate is slightly less vibrant. There's now more voice acting. But you get the same sense of wonder over the environment and the feeling that the story is much more than just "don't die." Definitely a steal at $20.

For fans of the original [i]Subnautica[/i]: consider this less of a sequel and more of an expansion pack; an additional campaign from the same game.  It has all the mechanics and gameplay of the original, but with a new story and environment to play in - and different props and vehicles to play with - it also has all of the same bugs and quirks, so don't expect it to be more polished than its progenitor.

Below Zero is a much more guided experience than the original (in a good way) - the experience unfolds from biome to biome significantly more naturally, and I never felt the need to reach for the wiki in the same way that I did with the original.  It is also, however, significantly smaller - both in direct scale and because 1/3 of the map is taken-up by above-ground snowy mountains and icebergs.

The above-ground gameplay, while not quite as bad as the original, is still this game's weakest point, and I was grateful when I had served my time in those monotonous mountainous mazes and could return to the more interesting underwater environments.  

With the map being that much smaller, though, the biomes you [i]do[/i] encounter are significantly smaller and fewer in number, making exploration feel much less rewarding; coupled with the game's more effective guidance, you end-up spending so little time in each biome that they never progress beyond feeling liminal.  

The game seems to encourage you to avoid lingering, too: the Seamoth and Cyclops have been replaced with a single submersible: the Seatruck, which can be extended with a variety of modules to obsolete almost every aspect of base-building, allowing you to perpetually stay on the move.  There's no functional reason to build a base beyond recharging batteries, so that aspect of the game has been relegated to an opt-in feature for those that enjoy it.

The leviathans and fauna, too, have been streamlined - their number and variety significantly reduced, and their behaviour homogenised - this has the effect of nullifying the horror aspect of the game from quite early on, as once you have the perimeter defence system up on the Seatruck, everything will leave you alone after a quick zap.  Where each creature from the original had a distinct call that could easily be identified, these new ones all fill the soundscape and blur into one, making aural scouting nigh impossible and removing that aspect of gameplay entirely.

Below Zero is a fine game and, for fans of Subnautica, it will scratch that [i]particular[/i] itch the series creates - but it doesn't hold a candle to the original and I would recommend it only to fans craving that underwater-exploration vibe.

This is exactly what you'd expect: the original Subnautica experience with a new world, new biomes, new monsters, new tools, new habitat components, an [i]excellent[/i] new soundtrack. And it's all wonderful.

In my opinion, the Below Zero biomes seem to flow more naturally into one another, and the progress is less predictable. In the first game, I sometimes felt like I was looking for one specific hidden passage somewhere that would lead me to the next depth level and the next tech tier. In Below Zero, the challenges are more varied. Some shallow areas can be quite dangerous. Some deep areas are quite safe and peaceful. There are multiple routes in and out of the cave systems.

The above-surface zones are a nice change of pace. The large open area you explore mid-game can feel a bit bland, if only because the new underwater biomes are so varied and gorgeous.

The new vehicle is great. [spoiler]The sea truck feels more balanced than the Cyclops from the first game; it's more akin to a customizable mobile base than an ass-kicking end-game novelty. The truck is unlocked fairly early and can be upgraded throughout the adventure.[/spoiler] 

There are several nice quality-of-life improvements. Renewable food can be found very close to the starter zone. The thermoblade is seemingly unlocked much earlier than in the original game (although my memory is fuzzy on that), which makes extended away trips much more fun and sustainable. [spoiler](For those who haven't played: the thermoblade lets you kill and insta-cook small fish as you come across them, so you can keep your vitals up.)[/spoiler] 

As of this writing, the campaign [i]scaffolding[/i] seems basically done. Much of the voice acting is incomplete, and some placeholder text remains (eg, a text blurb might say "Robin and Alan discuss their feelings about X".) But you can absolutely work through the story and tech progression and still have a pretty good idea of what's happening, filling in the gaps with your own imagination.

If, like me, you're more into the exploration and discovery, the game is basically ready to enjoy. If you prefer to have a directed adventure experience, I'd give it another few months.

Strongly recommended.

Firstly, I would like to say that Below Zero is by no means a bad game. It's definitely enjoyable and well worth checking out, but I can't help comparing to its predecessor and feeling like Below Zero just doesn't measure up.

Let's start with the positives. The map is absolutely stunning visually and I was constantly in awe of its beauty. Another thing I really enjoy is the expanded variety of edible plants. I must also say I really enjoyed the Al-An story. Unlike many other reviewers, I found the inclusion of NPCs a nice touch, namely a certain grandma who is made of 100% pure badass. The addition to things you can build on the base is very convenient, especially the Large Room. Lastly, many creatures are very cute and I appreaciate that.

Moving on to things that could be good but they would require a few touchups. 

First, the Seatruck. Love the idea, not a massive fan of the execution. The ability to customize it with modules is really good on paper, but some modules are just straight up useless - the aquarium and the sleeper module come to mind. The storage module could use some more space. There is so little storage that it makes longer trips extremely inconvenient, requiring at least two storage modules if you want to take along more loot than what you need to play through the story. 

Since I'm on the topic of vehicles, I can't let the Snowfox go unmentioned. A hoverbike sounds great on paper but the controls are awful. It feels extremely clunky and unresponsive at the best of times and straight up requires the jump module to do anything, meaning you can't use any other upgrades. It feels like something that would be great to cover vast expanses of open space, but it's meant to be used on very diverse land with a lot of obstacles. I ended up fully ditching it and just running everywhere on foot instead. If the controls could be adjusted, it would help a lot. 

Then there are the Precursor artifacts. Once again, great idea, not the best execution. I ended up having to look some things up on the wiki, which is never a good sign. I have absolutely no idea how I was supposed to find some of the that Al-An didn't give me coordinates to (and some he did point me to).

I'm very torn on the streamlining of the game, because at times it feels straight up excessive. While I understand that it's a good thing that the player isn't forced to run across the entire map back and forth all the time, it seemed like I needed absolutely no preparation for anything. Going to the cold places? You don't even need the cold suit or any warming food, there are enough peppers on location to keep you warm. There seems to be little to no need for preparation. I'm usually not one to complain about games being too easy, but Below Zero went a little overboard with the handholding there. 

Another gripe I have is with the Sam side of the story. It has some great and very interesting elements but it feels unfinished. I played through all of it, found the vast majority if not all the story related PDAs and I'm still not clear on what exactly happened to her or why she just didn't handle certain things herself, seeing as she clearly had the means. Same goes for the Mercury II, it just needs a bit of a push and it will be really great.

The last thing in the good-but-not-quite-great category would be the sound design. The music is very enjoyable, but there are small things with the sound design that just don't sit right with me, those being creature roars. In OG Subnautica, the roars of every predator feel very distinct and clue you in as to which creatures you may be dealing with if you head into certain places. In Below Zero, all of the sounds feel incredibly similar. Is it the cryptosuchus or the chelicerate roaring? I couldn't tell you. This leaves especially the leviathans feeling quite underwhelming and much less memorable.

There is really one thing I straight up dislike about Below Zero and that is how painfully short the game is. The map is tiny and even the fact that most of it is winding, confusing caves, doesn't manage to make up for it. Even while I spent about half my playtime on my first playthrough after the Seaworthy update being lost in said winding caves, it still took me only 15 hours to get through the entire thing (compare that to 35 in Subnautica). The map design also doesn't really provide any incentive to build bases (it's fast to traverse + there is a serious lack of nice spots) or really grow any plants because of how plentiful food and resources are. The deeper parts being small, tight caves full of obstacles also mean it's plain not worth it to build or use the Prawn suit. Unfortunately, I don't think this is something that can or will be changed at this stage of development, but it is a detriment to an otherwise really solid game.

If you liked Subnautica but thought it needed 1/3 of the game to be barely-traversible land segments set in identical white corridors and a protagonist who constantly says 'Erm... well that just happened' while the alien in her head constantly says stuff like 'this human concept of "hope"... i find it illogical', coupled with an unsatisfying story that gets derailed pretty much immediately in favor of a side story with a pointless conclusion, you'll probably be able to tolerate Below Zero long enough to beat it. For the love of god let Subnautica 2 be good
Although it has its own issues, its a perfectly functional game which would have been amazing as a standalone, but suffers from having to be a sequel to an excellent game.

I have a hard time recommending Below Zero to anyone except the most hardcore Subnautica fans. The whole game has so many downright strange design decisions, and compared to it's incredible predecessor I can't help but feel like it's a bit of a disappointment.

-In the original game, you were alone. Everyone on your ship is dead, and your one chance of escape was detonated in front of you. The only voice you're allowed to hear outside of the data logs of your dead friends is a cold, unfeeling AI (at least up until the very end). In Below Zero, a few hours in you'll always have AL-AN chilling in your subconscious. The main character talks too, and she's... just incredibly unlikable. After awhile, her dialogue lines really started to grate on me. The weirdest part is this wasn't a problem in early builds! She used to bounce off AL-AN and her sister pretty well. A shame they butchered her character in the full release.

-The ocean was vast and terrifying in Subnautica. Everything felt unknown and scary. In Below Zero, the map is tiny, and it's very rare I actually got unnerved by anything. Now, I wouldn't have a problem with the smaller map if they put that development time into making the sea much more densely packed and interesting, but instead, they focused on the Arctic, which ended up releasing as a broken, unfinished mess of a surface area. I have no idea how they did it, but they somehow managed to make a [i]hoverbike[/i], the [i]coolest vehicle ever conceived[/i], feel kinda lame to drive. It's almost impressive.

-Speaking of vehicles and not being fun, that applies to all of them. The zippy Seamoth has been replaced with the slow and bulky Seatruck, which is a very cool concept but isn't fun to actually pilot. The Prawn Suit is also a  major downgrade from the original game, with the Grappling Hook being heavily nerfed due to the developers patching out the fun movement tech that it provided. Despite the world being so much smaller it takes an artificially long time to travel from point A to point B due to these changes. In Subnautica it wasn't often I had to face one direction and hold down the W key for longer than a minute, but in Below Zero it happened [i]frequently[/i].

-Also, despite being much smaller, the world manages to be much more confusing somehow. Useful blueprints are stuck in really obscure positions, important areas can be easily missed if you're not poking into every crack in the terrain, and fragments can get very annoying to find (there were several occasions where I'd spend upwards of an hour searching for one or two fragments despite already being in the biomes they spawned inside).

-I'm not going to get into the story, but... I don't really like it, personally.

It really sucks that this game turned out like this, as there's still glimmers of Subnautica in there, deep down. The soundtrack is fantastic; I'm a big fan of Ben Prunty's work and he took the helm gracefully here. The environments are also beautiful, and areas like the Tree Spires and Twisty Bridges really have that mysterious, beautiful charm of the first game. Unfortunately, that charm never lasted long, as instead of focusing on those areas the game spends far too much forcing you into the terrible Arctic sections and prodding you towards the next goal of the complete mess of a story it has.

If you really, really, [i]really[/i] loved Subnautica, and are willing to look past this game's flaws just to get something close to it, then sure, I'd recommend Below Zero. I genuinely do think it has some good aspects, but they are greatly overshadowed by the flaws. Otherwise, just play (or replay!) the first game, it's leagues better.

Great, immersive, fun and a bit of a step-down from the previous game.

Graphics were improved in many ways. The world continues to look wonderful, the creatures, the flora, everything looks great and detailed. The weather system adds a lot of immersion with the storms, auroras, fog, etc.

Sound effects continue to be awesome and immersive. All the voice acting is great. And the music is excellent, also the jukebox tunes are great.

Gameplay was a bit of a step-down from the previous game. Starting the game on land, and having to spend a lot of time on land during important parts of the game, in a game named Subnautica, was very disappointing. Part of the magic that the first game had was the endless ocean all around you, and the feeling that you experienced is just lost in this one, when you are surrounded with land and icebergs full of friendly penguins.
Resource gathering and basic survival stays mostly the same, although this one felt more rushed. Some of the tools and upgrades that in the first game you had to do a lot of exploration to find, in this one you find pretty fast, making some of them unrewarding and even pointless.
The fauna continues to be interesting, with new fun additions, and for the most part not that aggressive or dangerous. The new leviathans are not that scary or dangerous as the ones in the previous game.
Resource availability in general is fine, with a few exceptions that you will notice pretty early. The distribution of resources on the biomes felt a bit off, I mean, finding almost endgame materials near the first biome was a bit disappointing.
The lack of a map in this game was even more painful than then first one, mainly on the land parts, but also underwater (the lack of the sonar was really painful). I still don't understand how an exploration game have no actual map (yeah, there is a map that is just a vague image of the land, and it's pretty much useless) to discover, add points of interest, rotate, zoom, etc.
Moving to the vehicles, losing the seamoth and cyclops was a heavy blow, I loved those. The replacements, are not so great. The sea truck pretends to be a mix of the two, offering the speed and versatility of the seamoth, and adding the "customizable mobile base" component of the cyclops with the modules. But in reality, it fails to deliver both. The size and shape of the sea truck makes it get stuck in all sort of places and is slower than the seamoth. The animation to get in and out is super annoying every time that you forget to park it tilted. And most of the modules are useless. Not only, they make the sea truck slower and less maneuverable, they offer little to no benefit. Only two of the six modules are really useful. If for some reason you still decide to build them all, you can't even park them in the sea truck dock, because every time you  leave, you have to manually detach the modules. The snowfox bike is just useless, weak annoying to drive, gets stuck on everything, can't ride over water, etc. Thankfully, we have our trusty prawn suit to save the day.
The building system continues to be great. There are a bunch of new tools, a TON of beds (seriously, how many beds can you build?), a lot of new buildable cosmetics, new cosmetic options for your base and a few new and redesigned machines.

The story has so much more focus this time, with a lot of voice acting, images of the characters that speak, characters background, etc. It was nice, not that interesting as the first one, but ok. Also, the order in which you find the PDA's hurt a lot the development of the plot, and maybe even leave you saying "what? that can't be right, i'm surely missing something".

Like the first game, there are a bunch of game modes to select when you start playing, depending on the experience you want to have. If you want more freedom to build and explore, or you want the survival elements as well, or you want to customize every aspect of it, there are modes for you.

In short, great and immersive game, it still has the core parts that made the first one so awesome, but is a bit of a step-down in many of the mechanics. If you enjoyed the first game, you probably will be a bit disappointed with this one, but you will enjoy it and have a lot of fun anyway.

tl;dr A solid follow up with some hiccups and downgrades.
