[h2][b][u]Recommendation:[/u][/b] Buy It (Perhaps on Discount)[/h2]
[b][u]tl;dr:[/u][/b] More of the great environments and collect-craft loop that the original [i]Subnautica[/i] gave, [i]Below Zero[/i] is a worthy companion game even if not a worthy successor. This game started out as DLC and that scope is reflected in the final product: lots of interesting new areas and creatures, but it is smaller and the land portion could have been ditched (not even replaced) without losing much. The story is good, but know that the larger cast (including NPCs!) gives a much different vibe than the lost-isolationist atmosphere that was a core part of the original.

Whether you, a fan of the original, should get this largely boils down to if the player-against-the-world feeling of the first was the main reason you loved it or not. If it was, this might disappoint and you should wait for a discount. If not--or if you even hated the relative silence--then you'll get great enjoyment out of this.

[h1]Thawing Out[/h1]
I feel it's important to address the story immediately. The planet, the general mechanics, and most items are carry-overs from [i]Subnautica[/i], so the largest changes are the story and the environments. [i]Subnautica[/i] was an astounding game for these two reasons: the story there was largely optional, told through PDAs and delayed broadcasts, making it largely about the player surviving and trying to figure out how to leave. Each new biome you discovered was an absolute treat, from the features to the caverns to the critters (and those PDAs/broadcasts were helpful in guiding the player towards new areas.) 

[quote=warning]Oh, right, if you haven't already had it drilled into your head: the best experience for both this and the original is playing as blind as you possibly can. I avoid spoilers in this review but you're still better off reading only the tl;dr and skipping the rest of this review if you think you'll play it.[/quote]

For [i]Below Zero[/i] the story is both better and worse. There are actually two main stories here, which intersect but never really intertwine. It's possible to beat the game without seeing one story out, and possible to complete that story without beginning the ending-critical one. They have good beats and interesting characters, but the interactions you'll have as protagonist Robin Ayou gives a very different focus than the lone-survivor aspect of [i]Subnautica[/i]. The low-key dread is gone, and to fill its place there are discussions about humans and flavor voice logs between people who are no longer around. Even without her eventual companion and the one other NPC, Robin is rather chatty and the very early game has her talking to herself in order to prompt the player about what to do next. While I liked the story and dialog, this hand-holding felt annoying (especially considering my time spent in [i]Subnautica[/i]). Thankfully, it doesn't last too long and for players who want to skip the later dialog most of it seems to be "optional". 

All environments in the game are new; the two exceptions would be a handful of smaller plants returning plus an equivalent to the Creepvine forest (though that still has unique changes). Many are just as beautifully crafted and awe-inspiring as the original... but there are fewer of them, and no in-game reason to return to half of them after an initial visit. A very large chunk of the playable area is taken up by an ice shelf, and about 20% of game time takes place on this. It's an obvious answer to "where do we go from a game that's largely underwater", but the entire shelf could have been cut with little loss. The leviathan-type creature that's there is simply annoying and the intended main method of traversal--the Snowfox--is difficult to control (and you get thrown from it whenever that creature appears, regardless of how close.) Despite being so huge, the biome variety is incredibly disappointing and it's quite easy to get lost. A few other biomes also feel like vast nothingness; the deepest two biomes, while initially astounding, completely lack internal variety except the one plot-point each that they contain.

All large creatures are new, with only some of the "cannon fodder" fish appearing in this side-quel. If you've played [i]Subnautica[/i] you already know how to use (and even mostly craft) 85% the tools and items you'll be using in the game. A great addition for those who love building bases is the "Large Room", where interior walls can be placed to section off rooms as desired.  For on the go, the only vehicle to carry over is my beloved PRAWN; the other two options are replaced by a modular Sea Truck. With sufficient modules, the Sea Truck makes a great home-away-from-home; it's an excellent addition despite some minor quibbles. Sadly I found the PRAWN less useful this time around; not that the functionality has changed, just that the scenarios that made it a go-to option in [i]Subnautica[/i] don't really apply here.

Because it's built on largely the same engine, [i]Below Zero[/i] has benefited from better execution: Even on my aging PC I experienced very little pop-in and the few bugs were annoying rather than game-breaking. There are still many areas where Robin will slide in because collision is too tight on some objects (such as rock piles) but I never got stuck in one like I did a few times in [i]Subnautica[/i]. The original game took me about 30 hours to complete and [i]Below Zero[/i] 25 hours, which included unnecessary sight-seeing (and wasting two hours right before the end of the game constructing a base that almost immediately became pointless.)

I greatly enjoyed my time in [i]Below Zero[/i] and recommend it to both fans of the original and new-comers while I do believe it is overshadowed by the base game. (Making this more "sub" and less "nautica", I suppose.)  I bought the EA at release for a cheaper price but I would have felt fine paying the current $30 MSPR; seeing as how the base game is the same cost, though, I can't fault someone for waiting on a discount before diving into [i]Below Zero[/i].

The development of this standalone expansion focused too much on adding features such as a character-driven story, weather mechanics and more land gameplay, but in exchange downgrading the key features that made Subnautica 1 so amazing.

Comparing Below Zero to the original (minor spoilers for the original ahead):

[b]Pros:[/b]

[list]
[*]The waters feel overall much more alive, fish AI has been improved, and the density of fish is higher. It's a lot more fun now to explore and interact with the little fish in the game. The predators' behavior is also improved to be a little more of a threat which is a good change over the previous title to keep the players feeling a sense of danger.

[*]The addition of freezing weather as another survival challenge is pretty cool. But unfortunately diving into the water warms you up, and there's not a lot of incentive to stay on the surface after exploring the few key locations. So the entire mechanic, and all its items to help you survive the harsh weather, feel a bit underwhelming.

[*] You can build bigger, nicer bases now, but seeing as the map is smaller with less to explore, there's no point to spend too much time on building a massive base (or multiple bases) in my opinion, unless it's only for the sake of it. I would use the real-life analogy of moving to a house with a much smaller living room (map to explore) but with a much bigger bathroom (bases you build). 
[/list]

[b]Cons:[/b]

[list]
[*]The protagonist has a personality and dialogue moments and the story is more engaging. However, the feeling is a little bit quirky/ cartoony with silly jokes and little to no serious emotions (which takes away from the tension of exploring a dangerous underwater world).

[*]You are no longer stranded in a vast open ocean, but rather you are in a body of water that is mostly surrounded by ice sheets, and you are by no means alone, the place feels more like an earth research site than a mysterious alien planet. There are no places with open-water, where you cannot see the seafloor or walls of rock around you (such as we had at the underwater islands in Subnautica 1). There is no extremely spooky dark cave system (such as we had when entering the blood kelp and getting really disoriented in the darkness, or even the spooky dark vibes of the jellyshroom cave and deep grand reef. All of the caves are really well lit and smaller in size. The land gameplay gets boring very quickly, it's mainly just ice sheets with some penguins and polar bear equivalents.
Overall, the map is smaller, less deep, less diverse, and less spooky. But still beautiful.

[*] Vehicles and handheld technology have been significantly downgraded. A lot of them cut out from the game. The new Seatruck feels clunky and has less available mods than even the seamoth from the previous title. 

[*] The density of predators is much higher now. There are few areas where you can cruise around relaxed and admire the environment instead of rushing through to get away from threats. It's fun that you can kill them quickly but it still gets annoying. Two biomes that are taking up the middle of the map (which you keep having to cross) are absolutely infested with medium sized predators at all depths (think crag field but with bonesharks also at the water surface level), and you'll get real tired of crossing the middle of the map. There is no tension buildup over exploring a distant dangerous biome, because the most dangerous biomes are right outside the safe starting area (with the exception of the end game biome).
[/list]

[b]Conclusion:[/b]

The creative direction took a turn away from what made Subnautica so intriguing and unique. The feeling is less of an open-world exploration in a vast ocean, and more of a linear story experience. The features added compared to the features removed/ downgraded don't constitute a net improvement to the fun of the game, albeit that it definitely feels refreshing. [b]The main charm of the game is mostly lost.[/b]

It's still one of the best survival/ crafting games out there, but I have to leave a negative review because it's too much of a downgrade from the original. I hope the team at Unknown Worlds decides to return back to their original Subnautica recipe, and expand upon it in a future sequel.

I enjoyed the original Subnautica a great deal, which is why I was confounded when its sequel, Below Zero, turned out to simultaneously be basically identical and way less enjoyable to me. I don't think the gameplay is the issue; it's the primary point of similarity to its predecessor, with a basically identical progression of underwater survival and construction that still works the way it's supposed to. The main changes are the replacement of the two submarines with a new submarine that is much less interesting, which is a downgrade but not a massive one, and the introduction of more on-land stuff, including a land vehicle that handles like ass and a temperature gauge, which are again mostly non-starters but not so much that it ruins the game. Then again, even though the moment-to-moment mechanical experience is about the same, it still dragged way more for me; this could be because the fundamental discovery and mystery and thrill of the original game, how it felt like you were eking out survival and learning to live against all odds, were so core to its appeal that the basic structure has next to no replay value. Regardless, a much easier-to-identify issue is the story, which tries to be more in-depth and character-focused and less about you and your basic survival than the previous game, and is wholly unconvincing. The characters are all annoying and uninspired, especially yours, and the plot is just dull and largely feels like it's going through the motions. There's also this unfortunate insistence on the sterile therapy-speak that's endemic in a lot of media that takes itself seriously nowadays, where characters just state their emotions and their healthy process of handling them with no ambiguity or real humanity on display, like it's a how-to pamphlet for how to get through traumatizing events and not a story about flawed, compelling people actually doing it. This, combined with my issues with the gameplay, meant that I was sick and tired of Below Zero well before the halfway point. I hate to be so down on it, because I liked the first game a lot and wanted to like this too, but it just never came together for me. Shame.

Below Zero does not want to be Subnautica, again.

This isn't a horror game, it is an exploration of a beautiful alien ocean. 
The BZ world is a wilderness, beautiful, entangled, and jungle-like. I loved exploring it, and just swimming around. It was great.

Below Zero fails terribly, in two respects. Story and trying to have a land segment. 
The land segment ( in a game called SUBNAUTICA ) that is over 20% of the map ( that could have been more wonderful freaking ocean ). And is the most boring, least interesting, most frustrating part of the game.

Story wise; I think they missed it pretty hard. I love the shift towards more chill exploration, but there really isn't much to build towards. The ending is neat, but comes very much out of no where. They were intent on having a story that wasn't about escape, but exploration. The voiced protagonist ( whom is not in and of herself bad ) has her goals and interactions, but they are very much separate from mine. I wanted to explore, and reach a conclusion. She flip flopped off her main goal very quickly.

This could have been better. Sadly, it isn't. None the less. Give it a go if it's on sale.

[h1]What This Game Does Right[/h1]
- The terrain and texture quality are miles ahead of the original.
- The weather and atmosphere make the game look better than the original. There was a lot of awkward loading in the original especially in the mountains region which made the original look pretty bad. The fog helps with this aspect tremendously.
- Base building is MUCH better in almost every aspect. It shows you when something is preventing you from building by highlighting obstacles in yellow. The new structures add a world of possibilities. Some of the structures are very gimmicky, but I can't complain much about being able to toy around with new possibilities.
- The ability to pin crafting recipes in the PDA is really helpful.
- Resource deposits and ore veins are a mechanic that I never thought I needed. Having ore specific deposits is great.

[h1]What This Game Does Wrong[/h1]
- Unlocking new technology is incredibly painful. A lot of the technologies are sprawled around the map with no rhyme or reason. In the original, the player could explore wrecks that served as landmarks, which make finding new technology more practical. In this game, you have to scrounge around biomes finding stray fragments that blend in with the ground or are covered entirely by grass.[spoiler]There are these big ship fragments in the world that make up for it, but this only accounts for like 5-10% of the total technology you can get.[/spoiler]
- THE SEA TRUCK IS BAD. I get it, some of you like the modularity of it, but it's just the worst parts about the Cyclops and the Seamoth wrapped into one. Without upgrades, it's slower than the Seamoth and maneuvers like a cruise ship in comparison. I get you can upgrade it, but then you start adding all the modules that make it functional, and it goes back to being awful again. You can't build inside the Sea Truck, the storage is abysmal, and you don't get the alternative camera angles like the Cyclops. Luckily the map is so small that having a slow vehicle doesn't impact progression much. Having the Seamoth/Cyclops in the original game was great, as you could have a speedy, highly maneuverable ship as well as a tanky mobile base at your disposal. The Sea Truck is none of that unfortunately.
- The leviathans are no longer scary. [spoiler]One of them looks like a giant shrimp, which is exactly as terrifying as it sounds[/spoiler]. Considering how small the map is, the concentration of enemies is almost too high.
- The enemies feel recycled, in a really bad way. The first time I saw a Ghost Leviathan in the original game, it was both terrifying and fascinating. In this game, I get chased by whales with teeth. All of the enemies look the same, in my opinion.

I get that it sounds like I am harsh, but I still like the game. It's an okay game, and it's one of the few times I was willing to pay full price for a game. However, it doesn't come close to the original, and I was honestly let down, albeit because my expectations were high. Would I still have bought it, yes, but I can't see myself getting 200+ hours out of it like the original. If you liked the exploration aspect or building aspect of the first game, you will enjoy this game as well. If you liked the original for the novelty aspect, being terrified by the creatures that inhabit Planet 4546B, or getting lost in the immensity of the ocean, I would stick with the original.

I [i]liked[/i] it.

But only because I played the original. I can't say I would become a fan of these games if I played Below Zero first.

I'll start with what is arguably better:

- New biomes look fantastic, especially the "snake biome" or "huge orange flowers biome", everything got more bioluminescent and it adds more charm to this game.

- More story focused but not too much, voiced protagonist, cutscenes, alive characters. But because of this particular story it feels like there is much less mystery going on, you kinda know everything about this world already.

- Dynamic weather: wind, fog, freezing rain, the impact of it on the water looks amazing.

- Seatruck.

Now the bad parts:

- TOO MUCH LAND. I get the appeal of adding more land to explore but this particular game just feels worse that way and land movement is clunky. The map itself feels smaller too. There is a Seafox hover bike but it doesn't feel good to use. The only land additions I liked are: Ice Worm leviathan and cold system. Also why would you explore more land in the game called Subnautica?

- Not scary. As I said, the map is too small and you pretty much know everything about the layout in first hours, no mystery so it doesn't feel like you're in any danger.

- Soundtrack, it's not bad, it is fitting but it's not unique. Here it feels like background ambiance while the original had so many bangers and could awoke interesting feelings. I hope that Subnautica 2 will have soundtrack at least on the level of the original.

Closing words:

I think it's a great expansion if you played the first game but you definitely shouldn't start with this one. Play it only if you crave more Subnautica or want to know more of the lore.

There's a lot of negative talk out there about BZ from fans of the original Subnautica - but in my opinion this is really coming from people who wanted BZ to be Subnautica again instead of its own game. BZ is meant to be moreso of a story driven exploration rather than Subnautica's semi indefinite survival. I think BZ expands on a lot of things that Subnautica never quite had the time to - each biome feels so much more alive with the density of fauna being a big contributor in my mind, though that does technically come at the expense of ecological realism. The map feels a lot less empty & more worth exploring, I personally think the smaller map size compared to Subnautica is an excellent decision because in Subnautica you legitimately had to frequently spend 10 minutes just holding down the W key in late game to travel to important locations. The voice acting and story aren't the deepest best thing ever or anything, but they're not meant to be the star of the game. My final note is I think the decorations are diverse enough to be worthwhile and usefulness of various items feels a lot more rewarding. Also the seatruck is cool
subnautica is better, but this game is still good
